text: The Service Value Chain's six activities aren't locked into one order, but a real request still moves through them in a recognizable path. This lesson follows one request — self-service password resets — from first ask to live operation.

Six activities: Plan, Improve, Engage, Design & transition, Obtain/build, Deliver & support. All six exist in every organization. This lesson shows one real path a substantial request takes through five of them, with Improve running the whole time.

Engage captures the request and the real need behind it. Plan weighs it against everything else competing for budget and time. Design & transition turns an approved idea into a tested specification and rollout plan. Obtain/build sources whatever that calls for — a license, an integration. Deliver & support runs the capability once live, handling what self-service can't resolve.

Improve isn't a seventh step at the end. Engage might flag a repeating request pattern. Plan might notice its own prioritization process is slow. Design & transition might notice the same defect category keeps appearing in testing. Deliver & support, once live, is most likely to notice the tool itself needs a fix.

ITIL 4 calls a specific combination of activities and practices for one scenario a value stream. Building that password-reset capability is a large value stream touching all six activities. A single user actually using it, once built, is a far smaller one — mostly Engage and Deliver & support.

The exam, and real incident, problem, and change work ahead, assume you can place any scenario on this chain without hesitating: capturing a need, deciding priority, specifying a change, sourcing a component, running operations, or feeding back an improvement.
